config.title: Lifting State Up

intro.title: Lifting State Up
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple counter app with two child components that need to share and update the same count value. You will learn the concept of 'lifting state up,' which involves moving shared state from child components to their closest common parent component. The main technologies and constructs you will use are Angular components, TypeScript for state management, and property and event binding for communication between parent and child components. By the end, you will understand how to manage shared state efficiently in an Angular application.
intro.usecase: In real-world Angular applications, lifting state up is essential when multiple components need to share and synchronize data. For example, in an e-commerce dashboard, product filters in a sidebar component must update the product list in the main content area—both components need access to the same filter state. Similarly, in a project management tool, changing a task's status in a modal should immediately reflect in the task board view. This pattern ensures consistent UI behavior across different parts of complex applications like admin panels, data visualizations, or multi-step forms where components are siblings or have a common ancestor.

objectives: Construct a parent component that manages shared state for child components
Initialize state in a parent component and pass it down to child components via property bindings
Configure child components to emit events when local state changes need to be communicated upward
Implement event handlers in the parent component to update the shared state based on child events
Bind the updated state from the parent back to child components to synchronize their displays
Integrate two-way data flow between parent and child components using @Input and @Output decorators
Manipulate the application structure to centralize state management in the appropriate parent component

steps.title: Import Component and CommonModule from Angular core
steps.instruction: Import the Component decorator and CommonModule from '@angular/core'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import multiple symbols from the same module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing Angular core decorators
import { Component, NgModule } from '@angular/core';
steps.expectedOutcome: The Component decorator and CommonModule are imported, making them available for use in your Angular application.
successCriteria: Component and CommonModule are imported from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing both Component and CommonModule from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackWrong: import both Component and CommonModule from the '@angular/core' module.

steps.title: Create the parent TemperatureCalculator component
steps.instruction: Create a new Angular component named TemperatureCalculator using the @Component decorator. Define a selector, template, and styles array. The template should be empty for now.
steps.hint: Use the Component decorator imported in the previous step. The selector can be 'app-temperature-calculator', template can be an empty string, and styles can be an empty array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TemperatureCalculator component class is created with the @Component decorator, an empty template, and empty styles array.
successCriteria: The TemperatureCalculator component is defined with @Component decorator, selector 'app-temperature-calculator', empty template, and empty styles array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've included all required parts: @Component decorator with selector, template, and styles properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you used @Component decorator with selector, template, and styles properties.

steps.title: Initialize temperature state in the parent component
steps.instruction: Inside the TemperatureCalculator component class, add a public property called 'temperature' with type number and initial value 20.
steps.hint: Add a property declaration in the class body, like 'temperature: number = 20;'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a temperature property initialized to 20, ready to be used for lifting state.
successCriteria: TemperatureCalculator class contains a public 'temperature' property with type number and initial value 20.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that the property is named exactly 'temperature', has type 'number', and is initialized to 20.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: you need to add a property called 'temperature' with type number and value 20 inside the TemperatureCalculator class.

steps.title: Create the child TemperatureInput component
steps.instruction: Create a new child component named TemperatureInput with a @Component decorator and an empty template.
steps.hint: Define a new class with @Component decorator, similar to the parent component but with a different selector.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new TemperatureInput component class is defined with @Component decorator and empty template.
successCriteria: TemperatureInput component is created with @Component decorator, a selector, and an empty template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the component, but make sure it has the @Component decorator with selector and template properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TemperatureInput component isn't properly defined. Check that you've created a class with @Component decorator.

steps.title: Add Input property to TemperatureInput component
steps.instruction: In the TemperatureInput component, add an input property called 'temperature' with type number using the @Input decorator.
steps.hint: Use @Input() temperature: number; inside the TemperatureInput class to receive data from the parent.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureInput component will have a temperature input property ready to receive data from the parent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you used the @Input decorator and specified the type as number.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TemperatureInput component should have an input property named temperature with type number.

steps.title: Create temperature update handler in TemperatureInput
steps.instruction: In the TemperatureInput component, add a method named onTemperatureChange that takes an event parameter and emits the temperatureChange output with the event's target value.
steps.hint: Define a method that handles the input change event and emits the new temperature value through the output property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureInput component now has a method that will handle temperature updates and emit them to the parent component.
successCriteria: TemperatureInput component contains an onTemperatureChange method that emits the temperatureChange event with the input value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your method properly emits the temperatureChange event with the input value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method isn't quite right. Remember to define onTemperatureChange that takes an event parameter and emits the temperatureChange output.

steps.title: Build TemperatureInput template with input field
steps.instruction: In the TemperatureInput component's template, add an input element with two-way binding to a local temperature property. Use [(ngModel)] for the binding and include a placeholder like 'Enter temperature'.
steps.hint: Add the input element inside the template string. Remember to import FormsModule if you haven't already, but for this step just focus on the template.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of an input with two-way binding in Angular
template: `<input type="text" [(ngModel)]="localValue" placeholder="Enter value">`
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureInput component will have an interactive input field in its template that can capture user input.
successCriteria: The TemperatureInput component template contains an input element with [(ngModel)] binding and a placeholder attribute.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input element, but make sure it has both [(ngModel)] binding and a placeholder attribute.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template should include an input element with two-way binding using [(ngModel)] and a placeholder.

steps.title: Wire input event to handler in TemperatureInput
steps.instruction: In the TemperatureInput component template, add an (input) event binding to the input element that calls the onTemperatureChange method with the input's value.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (input)="onTemperatureChange($event.target.value)" on the input element.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: binding an input event to a handler
<input (input)="handleInput($event.target.value)" />
steps.expectedOutcome: The TemperatureInput component's template now has an input element with an (input) event binding that triggers the onTemperatureChange method.
successCriteria: The input element in the TemperatureInput template includes (input)="onTemperatureChange($event.target.value)".
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using Angular's event binding syntax (input) and passing the input value to onTemperatureChange.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input event isn't properly bound. Check that you're using (input)="onTemperatureChange($event.target.value)" on the input element.

steps.title: Add TemperatureInput to parent template and wire data flow
steps.instruction: In the TemperatureCalculator component's template, add the TemperatureInput component with property binding for temperature and event binding for temperatureChange.
steps.hint: Use the child component selector with square brackets for property binding and parentheses for event binding.
steps.expectedOutcome: The parent component template now includes the child component with two-way data binding.
successCriteria: TemperatureInput component is used in TemperatureCalculator template with property binding for temperature and event binding for temperatureChange.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added the TemperatureInput component, but make sure both property binding and event binding are correctly implemented.
steps.feedbackWrong: The TemperatureInput component is not properly wired in the parent template. Check the syntax for property and event binding.
